final_recommendation: The room converged on a protocol amendment with independent monitors, automatic monthly reporting, and tariff suspension on named product lines tied to labor violations. Mexico accepted enforcement mechanisms with sovereignty safeguards (Mexican inspectors present, Mexico schedules inspections), Congress committed to a vote within 14 days of text finalization, and Canada agreed to ratify without reopening other provisions.
minority_objections: Mexico initially resisted unannounced facility access as sovereignty violation, insisting on scheduled inspections with Mexican inspectors present
Congress initially demanded unannounced access and no cure period, later accepted 30-day remediation window as compromise
key_conflicts: Unannounced vs. scheduled facility inspections (sovereignty vs. enforcement teeth)
Automatic tariff suspension with no cure period vs. 30-day remediation window
Independent monitors with final say vs. joint Mexico-monitor teams
Timeline pressure: media/business demanding immediate announcement vs. need to finalize legal text
key_concessions: Mexico accepted independent monitors with facility access and automatic reporting in exchange for Mexican inspectors being present and Mexico scheduling inspections
Congress accepted 30-day remediation window instead of immediate automatic suspension
Labor accepted monitors observing rather than unilaterally triggering inspections
Canada committed not to reopen dairy or Chapter 19 in exchange for labor-only amendment
red_lines: Congress: no ratification without automatic tariff triggers and independent verification
Mexico: no unannounced inspections without Mexican government presence (sovereignty)
Canada: no reopening of dairy concessions or Chapter 19 dispute settlement
Labor: no ratification if Mexico retains unilateral veto over enforcement findings
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Implementation capacity: no discussion of whether Mexico has institutional capacity to meet monthly reporting and rapid remediation timelines
Political sustainability in Mexico: minimal exploration of domestic Mexican political backlash to perceived U.S. oversight
Precedent effects: limited discussion of how this enforcement model might affect future trade agreements or other USMCA provisions
Business disruption: tariff suspension on named products could disrupt supply chains, but room focused on legal mechanics over operational impact
downstream_risk_variables: Mexico's actual implementation of labor reforms and ability to meet 30-day remediation timelines
Congressional vote margin: whether 14-day timeline is sufficient for caucus whipping
Public narrative stability: whether media framing as 'labor victory' holds or shifts to 'sovereignty compromise'
Canadian domestic reaction to U.S.-Mexico bilateral labor deal without Canadian input on enforcement design
Business lobby acceptance of tariff-suspension mechanism as predictable vs. arbitrary
uncertainty_notes: Final legal text not yet signed; Mexico's commitment to 'scheduled inspections with monitors present' vs. Congress's demand for 'automatic enforcement' leaves ambiguity on who triggers inspections in practice. Timeline for actual ratification vote (14 days) is aspirational but not locked. Media narrative could shift if implementation details leak before joint announcement.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Opening statement: 'votes don't exist to pass this deal as written'; entire meeting structured around unlocking ratification through amendment; drove every exchange
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Labor union and Congress repeatedly demanded independent monitors, automatic tariff triggers, no cure period; shaped amendment design from R1 through R5; central driver
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Business demanded 14-day vote timeline and joint announcement for certainty; conditioned support on closing deal quickly; genuine pressure but not dominant thread
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Canada stated red line on dairy/Ch19 reopening and committed to ratify labor-only amendment; real consideration but secondary to U.S.-Mexico labor negotiation
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Mexico's core objection throughout: unannounced inspections = sovereignty violation; insisted on Mexican inspectors present; drove compromise language on scheduled vs. unannounced access
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Media actor set 45-minute deadline, framed as 'labor victory' vs. 'Mexico blocks'; created urgency but did not drive substantive enforcement design
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Entire meeting premised on 'deal fails without amendment'; Canada's warning that reopening risks unraveling whole package; stability contingent on ratification compromise was the room's foundation
